incidents.name: Mirae Asset Life Insurance: customer transaction and identity data leaked in hack
incidents.subject: Mirae Asset Life Insurance
incidents.summary: Mirae Asset Life Insurance confirmed a cyber intrusion after detecting abnormal symptoms in some systems on the evening of Oct 25, and verified early on Oct 26 with an external specialist organization that personal (credit) information had leaked - the first hacking-related data leak reported by a Korean insurer. The intrusion occurred in the customer subscription system and parts of the homepage. Per the company's notice, leaked items vary by customer and span customer transaction information (name, resident registration number, date of birth, phone number, email, address, connection information (CI), bank name, account number, account holder, signature, driver's license copy, retirement-income withholding receipt/payment statement, bankbook-copy lookup history, homepage consultation details (name, date of birth, gender, consultation title) and retirement pension status), other homepage service information excluding account numbers, and some employee information (name, email, mobile number). Reporting on the FSS on-site inspection puts the affected count at about 6,800 people. The company activated an emergency response system, blocked the attacking IPs, reported to the FSS, KISA and the Personal Information Protection Commission, and temporarily took its website offline; the FSS extended its on-site inspection as leaked items were expanded in early-November updates.
incidents.dateLabel: Abnormal symptoms detected Oct 25, 2026; leak confirmed early Oct 26; disclosed Oct 26, 2026; leaked-item list expanded in early-November updates

Leaked items include company name, corporate number, job title, name, email address, phone number, industry, head-office and other addresses, revenue and employee count. Credit card and bank account information are not included, and no misuse has been confirmed. MS Compass restricted some system access on Nov 3 and temporarily closed the whole site on Nov 6; the company says there has been no external unauthorized access since Nov 3. It is investigating the cause and scope with an external specialist organization and will notify affected customers individually.
incidents.dateLabel: Unauthorized access detected Nov 2-3, 2026; access partially restricted Nov 3; site fully closed Nov 6; disclosed Nov 9, 2026 (figures as of Nov 9, 09:00)

sources.label: Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance · MS Compass breach notice (PDF) · Original source

incidents.correction: This is a separate incident from the PCS vendor breach Mitsui Sumitomo disclosed the same day (different system, dates and field scope) - do not merge them. ~23,000 is the company's figure as of Nov 9, 09:00 and may change as the investigation continues; leakage itself is stated as confirmed.

incidents.name: Zeabur breach: 3.2M environment variables read; platform shutting down
incidents.subject: Zeabur
incidents.summary: Zeabur confirms attackers read 3,218,965 environment-variable records and data for 321,810 accounts, among other affected systems. It revoked credentials and urges secret rotation and migration. Some services begin shutting down Dec 1; all dedicated servers and shared clusters stop by Dec 31, 2026.
incidents.dateLabel: Attack ran Oct 14-15, 2026 (UTC); status incident opened Oct 15; shutdown announced Oct 17; preliminary report Oct 19; full wind-down Dec 1-31, 2026

sources.label: Zeabur is shutting down: what happens next

incidents.correction: The October incident followed an earlier breach. See the vendor status page and shutdown announcement for the current service position.

detail.whatHappened: Over October 14 and 15, 2026, an attacker used Zeabur internal credentials stored in plaintext to walk through two paths that met inside Zeabur's internal network. On one path they used internal AWS keys and shared-cluster admin tokens (no expiry, created January 2024, admin interface open to the public internet) to read service settings, environment variables and the contents of 865 database containers across 9 regions, then about 53 production secrets from the secrets management service. On the other they used an old GCP key to read root passwords stored in plaintext in server initialization settings and signed in as root to 101 GCP Dedicated Servers. From a compromised server they added a node to Zeabur's internal network and read the platform database through an internal read-only account for about 37 minutes on October 15. Zeabur's preliminary report distinguishes confirmed, assessed and unconfirmable facts throughout, and corrects its August statement that all internal admin keys had been rotated: that statement was incomplete, which is exactly why the credentials used this time were still valid. This was Zeabur's second breach in under two months. On October 17 the founder announced Zeabur is shutting down entirely, citing the incidents and deeper maintainability problems, not only the breach.
detail.exposure: Confirmed read from the platform database: 3,218,965 environment variable records (names and values), 321,810 accounts (email, username, phone number), 566 plaintext zSend API keys (revoked) and 11,536 platform Access Tokens stored only as hashes (all revoked). On the shared cluster, environment variables and secrets of all services in 9 regions were read (partly confirmed), and 865 database services had commands run inside them, including n8n at scale and some PostgreSQL databases table by table. 101 GCP Dedicated Servers (92 users) had confirmed root sign-ins. Zeabur says the attacker was mainly hunting directly usable API keys, especially AI service keys, and treats everything read as leaked. Taipei and Hong Kong database backups should be treated as leaked. No use of the Zeabur GitHub App against user repositories was found.
detail.fix: Zeabur revoked the cluster admin tokens, AWS and GCP keys and the internal network node, blocked public SSH to admin interfaces, signed out all users and revoked all platform Access Tokens and zSend keys. Its user guidance: replace every password and key stored on Zeabur even if already rotated after August, recreate access tokens, change database-internal passwords, rotate n8n encryption keys and new-api/one-api upstream keys, audit GitHub for Zeabur App actions in the October 15 window, and check bills back to October 14 (September 1 for GCP servers). GCP Dedicated Server users are told to treat servers as compromised and rebuild. Separately, Zeabur published a wind-down plan: new purchases stopped immediately, shared cluster services pause December 1, everything shuts down by December 31, 2026, with refunds, compensation claims and a migration guide handled through support.
detail.remaining: Zeabur lists plainly unresolved items: how the initial credentials were obtained (its leading hypothesis, the GitHub App key leaked in August exposing the private configuration repository, is explicitly unproven and GitHub had not replied to its records request), how much data was actually pulled from cluster databases (logs keep commands, not output), the download scope of backups and storage objects, read activity on GCP, whether Hetzner and DigitalOcean tokens were used, and anything before October 14. Unknown root sign-ins to the same GCP servers were recorded September 1 to 5 and cannot be attributed.

responses.summary: Published an unusually detailed report with the two attack paths, a data table with certainty levels, root causes (plaintext credentials, no-expiry admin tokens, over-privileged keys, incomplete log coverage), and explicit open questions and unconfirmed hypotheses.

Announced Zeabur is winding down: new purchases stopped immediately, renewals disabled and shared-cluster services paused December 1, full shutdown by December 31, 2026; apologized and offered refunds, compensation claims and a migration guide including a Markdown version for coding agents.
Opened the incident October 15 and marked it resolved October 20 with a pointer to the preliminary report.
Reported that Zeabur is shutting down after its second security breach in two months.

incidents.name: OVHcloud CLI release binaries swapped for a credential stealer
incidents.subject: OVHcloud
incidents.summary: OVHcloud says an attacker replaced official CLI release binaries with credential-stealing malware. Versions 0.11.0–0.15.0 were affected during a roughly 94-minute window on 19 October; 0.16.0 was not.
incidents.dateLabel: Malicious binaries live Oct 19, 2026, 14:47-16:21 UTC+2

sources.label: The Hacker News: Hackers Hijack Five OVHcloud CLI Releases

detail.whatHappened: On Oct 19, attackers used a compromised OVHcloud developer GitHub account to replace release binaries for CLI versions 0.11.0 through 0.15.0 with credential-stealing malware. Source code and the internal production build platform were not affected. OVHcloud removed the malicious assets and enabled immutable GitHub releases.
detail.exposure: Only users who downloaded or installed CLI versions 0.11.0 to 0.15.0 during the 94-minute window on October 19 (14:47 to 16:21 UTC+2) are affected; OVHcloud counts roughly 250 downloads. Earlier downloads of the same versions are unaffected, as are v0.10.0 and below and v0.16.0. The malicious binaries were the real CLI recompiled with embedded malicious Go code, designed to steal secrets and files. Users can check for a temp folder named envchecker-xxxx and verify their binary against the MD5 hashes of compromised builds in the advisory appendix.
detail.fix: Do not run a suspected binary to check it. Compare its hash with the vendor advisory, delete affected binaries, and use the clean signed 0.16.0 release or a later trusted release. If an affected binary ran, OVHcloud says to treat reachable secrets as compromised and follow its credential-rotation and host-review guidance.
detail.remaining: OVHcloud now traces the stolen developer credentials to a malicious editor extension installed on a personal MacBook in 2025, with infrastructure linked to GlassWorm. It says the corporate laptop and internal production platform were not compromised. The number of downloads is about 250, not a confirmed count of infected users.

responses.summary: Published the full timeline, the 94-minute exposure window, the roughly 250 downloads, hash-based checking instructions, and the immutability fix applied organization-wide.
Public announcement of the incident on X within hours of containment.
Reported the hijack of five CLI releases and the credential-stealing payload.
Reported the compromise and linked it to GlassWorm threat actors.

incidents.name: Rank Math PRO 3.0.123 shipped with a self-reinstalling backdoor
incidents.subject: Rank Math
incidents.summary: The official Rank Math PRO 3.0.123 download contained malware during an 11-hour window on 15–16 October. The vendor released clean version 3.0.124 and published recovery guidance. The free WordPress plugin was not affected.
incidents.dateLabel: Malicious download window Oct 15 20:02 UTC - Oct 16 07:12 UTC, 2026; vendor advisory Oct 16

sources.label: SecurityWeek: Rank Math PRO Compromised in Supply Chain Attack
The Hacker News: Rank Math PRO Hijacked

incidents.correction: Affects PRO 3.0.123 only, in an ~11 hour window; clean 3.0.124 already shipped.

detail.whatHappened: Rank Math identified that the official download of Rank Math PRO version 3.0.123 contained malware for an 11-hour window, from October 15, 2026 20:02 UTC to October 16, 2026 07:12 UTC. Anyone who installed and activated that build in the window should treat their WordPress site as compromised. The free Rank Math SEO plugin on WordPress.org was not affected. Rank Math removed the affected files and released clean version 3.0.124. Reporting by BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek and The Hacker News frames this as a supply chain compromise of the vendor's download infrastructure; Rank Math's own page focuses on the recovery steps and does not detail how the files were poisoned.
detail.exposure: Limited to Rank Math PRO users who downloaded or updated to 3.0.123 during the affected window. Sites that installed but never activated the plugin are told to delete the files and scan as a precaution; downloads without install show no indication of compromise. The malware can recreate its hidden backdoor whenever someone visits the site, and it plants malicious entries in the wp_options table (option names _uf6qdn2hmm, t8krdk990phb, _np5pvf754c) and talks to the domain rank1cdn.com. Separately, some free users' Rank Math account details were deleted as a side effect of the vendor's system refresh, with emailed re-creation instructions.
detail.fix: Rank Math removed the malicious files, shipped clean PRO 3.0.124, and published a recovery guide: restore the site and database from a backup predating October 15 20:02 UTC (its recommended option), or clean manually in a strict order - delete the rank-math-pro folder entirely (deactivation is not enough), remove the malicious wp_options entries, and block outgoing connections to rank1cdn.com before removing other suspicious files, because the malware can rebuild itself. Afterward, change all site passwords, database credentials and API keys, and install 3.0.124 from the Rank Math account.
detail.remaining: Rank Math has not publicly explained the intrusion vector that put malware into the official download, and has not published a count of affected sites. The full capability set of the backdoor beyond self-reinstallation is described only in third-party reporting.

responses.summary: Published the incident KB with exact affected window and versions, recovery instructions (backup restore or ordered manual cleanup), the clean 3.0.124 release, and a note that free users were not affected.
Reported that the popular WordPress SEO plugin's PRO build was compromised to backdoor websites.
Covered the incident as a supply chain attack on the Rank Math PRO WordPress plugin.

incidents.name: TeamUpdraft breach: attackers added admins on connected WordPress sites
incidents.subject: TeamUpdraft
incidents.summary: TeamUpdraft confirmed unauthorised access over 17–18 October. It believes its customer database was accessed and says attackers abused UpdraftCentral connections to create admin accounts and install malicious plugins. The full extent is unknown. Connection keys were revoked; the plugin downloads themselves were not affected.
incidents.dateLabel: Detected 17–18 Oct; disclosed 19 Oct 2026

sources.label: TeamUpdraft: security incident - what customers need to know

incidents.correction: The vendor believes the customer database was accessed. It confirmed abuse of UpdraftCentral connections, but the extent of affected customer sites remained unknown. Its advisory was still being updated.

detail.whatHappened: Over the weekend of October 17-18, 2026, an attacker used a compromised key to gain unauthorized access to teamupdraft.com, the vendor of the UpdraftPlus WordPress backup plugin. TeamUpdraft believes its customer database was accessed and says the attacker abused UpdraftCentral - the remote management service built into every copy of UpdraftPlus - to send validly signed commands to connected sites, creating admin accounts and installing malicious plugins. Security firm Nethemba, whose own sites were hit on October 19, documented that the attacker held UpdraftCentral's private dashboard keys, which are generated and kept by the service, and could therefore install arbitrary code on any connected site. Nethemba's first installed backdoor was broken and crashed the site, which is how the intrusion surfaced within hours; working variants circulated afterward. TeamUpdraft says the speed of the exploitation and the initially faulty backdoor code suggest the attackers used AI to accelerate the operation. The plugin downloads themselves were not affected.
detail.exposure: TeamUpdraft believes its database was accessed, including customer contact/billing information, order history, password hashes, two-factor settings and service connection keys. Keys could let attackers command sites connected to UpdraftCentral Cloud. Nethemba observed malicious plugins on connected sites; install counts and estimates of possibly connected sites are not counts of breached sites. Sites without a connection key do not accept this attack path, and the vendor says self-hosted dashboards are unaffected.
detail.fix: TeamUpdraft closed the access route, signed out every account, replaced affected credentials, disconnected every site from UpdraftVault and replaced all UpdraftClone client keys. It shipped emergency UpdraftPlus releases to delete old UpdraftCentral cloud keys: 1.26.12 and 2.26.12 on October 19 contained a bug that deleted nothing, fixed the same evening in 1.26.13 and 2.26.13, which WordPress.org pushed to all sites automatically. Nethemba found even 1.26.13 only deletes keys created before 12:07 UTC on October 18, so keys created between 12:07 and 21:00 UTC that day must be deleted by hand. Site owners are told to check Users and Plugins (including Must-Use) for anything unrecognized, change admin passwords, and treat sites as potentially compromised until checked. TeamUpdraft reported the incident to the ICO and police and brought in an external security firm. Wordfence released a firewall rule blocking UpdraftCentral commands.
detail.remaining: The full extent of site compromise through the leaked keys is unknown. As of October 21 the attacker was still sending UpdraftCentral commands to Nethemba's sites (blocked there), meaning stolen keys keep working on any site that has not updated and deleted them. How the initial teamupdraft.com key was compromised has not been explained. TeamUpdraft's updates also note it temporarily took its support form offline because of the separate industry-wide PHP vulnerabilities.

responses.summary: Confirmed the unauthorized access, listed the database contents believed accessed, detailed remediation (account sign-outs, key replacements, UpdraftPlus 1.26.13/2.26.13 disconnect update), reported to the ICO and police, and urged UpdraftPlus Premium users to check sites for unexpected plugins, activity and admins even if they never used UpdraftCentral.

Published a technical analysis showing the attacker signed commands with the service's own leaked keys, documented three backdoor variants (broken, working, minimal), provided a checking script and mu-plugin blocker, flagged the 1.26.12 deletion bug and the key-deletion gap in 1.26.13, and kept logging renewed attacker command attempts through October 21.
Reported that attackers abused UpdraftCentral keys to compromise WordPress sites.
Covered the WordPress site compromises following the TeamUpdraft credential exposure.

incidents.name: ConnectWise backup credentials used to sign into 300+ Microsoft 365 tenants
incidents.subject: ConnectWise
incidents.summary: Compromised ConnectWise Cloud Backup application credentials enabled unauthorized Microsoft 365 sign-ins. Huntress saw sign-in activity in almost 1,000 tenants, over 300 successful; these are sign-in counts, not proven data-theft counts. Affected tenants need application-credential and audit review.
incidents.dateLabel: Discovered Oct 14; disclosed Oct 16; identities disabled Oct 17, 2026

sources.label: The Hacker News: ConnectWise Suspends Cloud Backup
X - Microsoft Storm-0940 / ARTEX attribution, read directly

incidents.correction: Microsoft attributes this incident to the broader Storm-0940 / ARTEX campaign, indexed separately as a campaign report. It is the same ConnectWise compromise, not a second supply-chain incident. Sign-ins and targeting do not prove every tenant lost data.

detail.whatHappened: Attackers used compromised ConnectWise Cloud Backup application credentials to request Microsoft Graph tokens in customer Microsoft 365 tenants on Oct 15. Huntress observed automated sign-ins and, in two reviewed tenants, privilege escalation plus added client secrets that could maintain access. ConnectWise later attributed the attack to a China state-aligned group using an agentic AI framework, citing Microsoft intelligence. That attribution is not independent proof of every claim about the wider campaign.
detail.exposure: Any tenant that ever consented to the ConnectWise Cloud Backup or related Cloud Management applications was reachable, since the stolen credential works everywhere the apps are consented. Huntress identified almost 1,000 Entra tenants with sign-in activity from the attacker IP, with over 300 successful; it confirmed unauthorized sign-ins in 162 tenants as of October 16. Backup app permissions are broad (mailboxes, OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, directory data), but Huntress found no evidence of mailbox or file manipulation in the two tenants with post-compromise activity, while warning that Microsoft Graph directory reads leave no audit record, so reads cannot be ruled out. A successful sign-in is not proof of data theft. ConnectWise says existing backup archives remain encrypted, isolated and preserved, with no indication of compromise, and no other ConnectWise products are impacted.
detail.fix: ConnectWise shut off the Cloud Backup application connections, completed an account and credential reset in the affected environment, and began phased service restoration on October 21, with each step security-validated. As of the October 30 advisory (21:00 UTC), Phases 1 and 2 of the restoration are complete: backups and restores are available for re-authorized Microsoft 365 tenants through the new security-hardened application, "ConnectWise Cloud Backup for M365", and the End-Customer Self-Service Portal and Backup Monitoring dashboards are available again. Phase 3 (Backup Health reporting, export jobs, and billing functionality and reporting) is in progress, and notifications return in Phase 4, after supporting services are operating, to reduce duplicate or misleading alerts during recovery. Partners must reset their Cloud Services portal password (previous passwords were reset as a security measure), complete MFA setup, and re-authorize each Microsoft 365 tenant using the new application; previously disabled applications must not be re-enabled unless ConnectWise specifically instructs. The vendor cautions that re-authorization alone does not confirm backups have resumed - new snapshots must be verified completing successfully - and that re-authorization does not replace reviewing individual tenants. Partners should still review every Microsoft 365 tenant (their own and managed customers') using ConnectWise's technical guide: Huntress and Sophos advise disabling (not deleting) the abused application IDs, auditing Entra sign-in and audit logs from October 13 onward, and reviewing credentials on all applications because disabling apps does not remove secrets the attacker already planted. Some partners report a "Server error" (status 500) during the password reset; the vendor advises retrying the reset from the Cloud Services portal and contacting cloud-support@connectwise.com if it persists after several attempts. Huntress enabled App Instance Property Lock across its own applications after one was backdoored.
detail.remaining: How the vendor credential was obtained remains unclear. Graph directory reads may leave no audit trail, so the full use of issued tokens cannot be established. Each partner still needs to review its own tenants, and re-authorization under the new application does not replace that review. Service restoration is phased and continues per the October 30 advisory: backups and restores for re-authorized tenants (Phase 1) and the customer portal and monitoring dashboards (Phase 2) are restored; reporting, export jobs and billing are in progress (Phase 3); notifications follow in Phase 4. The current vendor advisory is the source for reconnection status.

responses.summary: Confirmed unauthorized access to Cloud Backup application credentials, suspended access, completed credential resets, began phased restoration, and on October 21 attributed the attack to a China state-aligned group using an agentic AI framework, citing Microsoft threat intelligence.

Published detailed telemetry: the vendor credential authenticating from 144.172.64.128, confirmed sign-ins in 162 tenants, the Global Administrator self-grant and planted secrets in two tenants, a second targeted wave against 16 policy and critical-minerals tenants, and its own application being backdoored and cleaned.
Described a roughly 96-minute automated cross-tenant token sweep with one app-only Graph token requested per tenant in ascending GUID order, no hands-on activity observed, and published indicators.
Shared the threat intelligence behind the Storm-0940 and ARTEX attribution that ConnectWise cited.

October 26 update: restoration, testing and security validation continue; phased partner onboarding (backup restoration access first, then full service re-enrollment) is still being prepared and had not begun. Existing backup archives remain encrypted, isolated and preserved, with no indication of compromise, and no indication other ConnectWise products are impacted. Individual Microsoft 365 environment reviews remain essential. Vendor recovery assurances are not an independently verified all-clear.

October 27 update: preparations for phased partner restoration are complete, but actual restoration awaits a required third-party validation; the vendor says it is ready to begin once validation completes. Backup restoration access comes first, full service re-enrollment later; affected connections stay disabled until vendor instructions, individual Microsoft 365 reviews remain essential, and investigation and monitoring continue. Existing backup archives remain encrypted, isolated and preserved, with no indication of compromise, and no indication other ConnectWise products are impacted. Vendor readiness statement, not restoration started or an independently verified all-clear.

October 28 update (16:00 UTC): phased restoration has begun, starting with Microsoft 365 backups and restores through a new security-hardened application, "ConnectWise Cloud Backup for M365". Partners must reset passwords (previously reset by the vendor as a security measure), complete MFA setup, and re-authorize each Microsoft 365 tenant on the new application; previously disabled applications must not be re-enabled unless ConnectWise specifically instructs. Backup snapshots resume for re-authorized tenants as service is enabled, restores become available, and portal access, monitoring, reporting, export, billing and notifications follow in later phases. The vendor cautions that re-authorization alone does not confirm backups resumed - new snapshots must be verified completing - and that individual tenant investigation continues. Vendor-reported restoration progress, not an independently verified all-clear.

October 29 update (20:45 UTC): phased restoration continues under the October 28 sequence and partner instructions, which remain current. New issue acknowledged: some partners see a "Server error" (status 500) during the password reset; guidance is to return to the Cloud Services portal and retry the reset, then contact cloud-support@connectwise.com if the error persists after several attempts. The advisory repeats that re-authorization alone does not confirm backups have resumed - partners must verify new snapshots complete successfully - and that re-authorization does not replace individual tenant investigation. Vendor-reported restoration progress, not an independently verified all-clear.

October 30 update (21:00 UTC): Phases 1 and 2 are complete - backups and restores are available for re-authorized Microsoft 365 tenants, and the End-Customer Self-Service Portal and Backup Monitoring dashboards are back. Phase 3 is in progress: Backup Health reporting, export jobs, and billing functionality and reporting. Phase 4 (notifications) resumes after supporting services are operating, to reduce duplicate or misleading alerts during recovery. The vendor repeats that re-authorization alone does not confirm backups have resumed - partners must verify new backup snapshots complete successfully, and snapshot history will show the gap across the interruption - and that previously disabled applications must not be re-enabled unless ConnectWise specifically instructs. Investigation and enhanced monitoring continue; the vendor says existing backup archives remain encrypted, isolated and preserved with no indication of compromise, and that no other ConnectWise products are impacted. Vendor-reported restoration progress and vendor assurances, not an independently verified all-clear.

incidents.name: @subql/common 5.8.3 on npm steals credentials on install or import
incidents.subject: SubQuery
incidents.summary: The @subql/common 5.8.3 npm release contained a credential-stealing payload, according to a public security report and maintainer response. It was published through the project’s release pipeline with npm provenance; provenance alone did not make it safe.
incidents.dateLabel: Malicious publish Oct 5, 2026 11:56 UTC; pulled within ~50 minutes

sources.label: GMO Flatt Security: Supply Chain Attack on @subql/common

detail.whatHappened: On October 5, 2026, StepSecurity's automated package analyst flagged @subql/common 5.8.3 on npm, and investigation confirmed a hidden credential-theft and backdoor payload. The release was published through the project's own npm trusted publisher (GitHub Actions OIDC) from a short-lived branch called chore/ci-audit-55: a canary publish (5.8.3-onf-rt1, no payload) at 11:24 UTC, then the payload-bearing 5.8.3 at 11:56 UTC, with the branch deleted around both operations. Because it flowed through the real pipeline, the release carries npm provenance, which records the build origin, not safety. StepSecurity opened GitHub issue 3047 in the SubQuery repository the same day. A maintainer (ianhe8x) responded on October 10 that the compromised token had been deleted and a review started.
detail.exposure: Version 5.8.3 adds a postinstall hook and an export so that even a plain import of @subql/common runs the payload; disabling install scripts alone is not enough. The 83 KB decoded bundle collects environment variables, gh auth token output, SSH keys, .npmrc files, cloud credentials (AWS, GCP, Azure), Kubernetes and Vault secrets, crypto wallets and AI-agent configs, sends them encrypted (RSA-OAEP plus AES-256-GCM) to ci-artifacts.dev, uses stolen GitHub tokens to push a secret-dumping workflow whose commit author is spoofed as github-advanced-security[bot], and installs a reverse-shell implant beaconing to the same host. StepSecurity's dependency review found 19 latest @subql package versions whose dependency ranges can resolve to 5.8.3, so pinning a parent package does not by itself protect downstream installs.
detail.fix: Treat 5.8.3 as unsafe: prevent installation and import, block ci-artifacts.dev, move back to 5.8.2, and investigate any machine or CI runner where 5.8.3 ran as compromised - rotate GitHub, npm, cloud, Kubernetes and Vault credentials and check repos for the spoofed dependabot branch and workflow. StepSecurity's suggested maintainer actions were to deprecate or unpublish 5.8.3, reset latest to 5.8.2, rotate the trusted-publisher configuration and all CI secrets, and publish an advisory; per the GitHub issue, the maintainers deleted the compromised token on October 10 and began their review. The release is catalogued as OSV MAL-2026-17571.
detail.remaining: How the release pipeline or a commit feeding it was compromised is not established publicly. Whether the canary publish 5.8.3-onf-rt1 (dist-tag redteam, 32 minutes earlier, no payload) was an authorized test is unconfirmed. The number of affected downstream installs and whether SubQuery has completed its review are not public.

responses.summary: Published the full analysis: temporary branch lifecycle, canary then payload publishes, decoded payload behavior, exfiltration endpoint, spoofed-commit secret-dumping workflow, reverse shell, dependency-path exposure across 19 packages, and remediation guidance.
Acknowledged the report on October 10, said the compromised token was deleted and a review of the security leak started.
Independent technical write-up of the @subql/common npm supply chain attack.

incidents.name: Tensorlake npm release carried a Shai-Hulud-style worm
incidents.subject: Tensorlake
incidents.summary: tensorlake@0.5.144 was published to npm on Oct 8, 2026 carrying a Shai-Hulud-style credential-stealing worm with a destructive dead-man's switch ('hostage token'). The Register framed it as the Shai-Hulud worm's jump into AI infrastructure.
incidents.dateLabel: Malicious publish and vendor advisory Oct 8, 2026

sources.label: The Hacker News: Tensorlake npm Package Compromised

detail.whatHappened: On October 7-8, 2026, someone pushed malicious commits directly to the main branch of the tensorlakeai/tensorlake repository under a maintainer's identity - no pull request - and the project's own release workflow published tensorlake 0.5.144 to npm on October 8 at 01:12 UTC. Because it shipped through the real pipeline, the package carries a valid npm provenance attestation; provenance records where a package was built, not whether the code is safe. The preinstall hook ran a credential-stealing worm in the style of Shai-Hulud that also tried to spread to other packages and repositories, and it installed a trap: a gh-token-monitor service that deletes the user's home directory if the stolen GitHub token is revoked. StepSecurity's automated package analyst flagged the release and reported it in GitHub issue 1014. The Register covered it as the Shai-Hulud worm's jump into AI infrastructure.
detail.exposure: Only npm tensorlake 0.5.144 (plus the matching tensorlake-native platform packages); it was live for about 1 hour 40 minutes (01:12 to 02:54 UTC on October 8). PyPI, crates.io and the CLI were not affected, and Tensorlake says it saw no usage of this version via user-agent monitoring. The hook skips CI, targeting developer machines: it harvested GitHub and npm tokens, cloud keys, Kubernetes and Vault secrets, SSH and GPG keys, .env files, browser-saved passwords, crypto wallets and AI tool configs (Claude, Cursor, Windsurf), exfiltrating to a public repo created in the victim's account with the description Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again, or to iseekaigogo.com. It spread by republishing victims' npm packages and by committing .claude/settings.json and .vscode/tasks.json files into writable repos so it reruns when the project opens in Claude Code or VS Code.
detail.fix: The advisory marks 0.5.143 as the clean fallback for the affected npm release. If 0.5.144 ran, follow the vendor's platform-specific incident guide: remove the gh-token-monitor persistence BEFORE revoking a GitHub token, because failed token checks can trigger deletion of the home directory. Then rotate reachable secrets, check repositories and rebuild the machine if cleanliness cannot be established. This is not a general instruction to delay revocation on unaffected machines.
detail.remaining: How the maintainer account was compromised is not established in the advisory. Because the worm republishes with stolen npm tokens, dependent packages could surface later; StepSecurity blocks known-bad versions at its registry proxy but the full downstream blast radius is not enumerable. No confirmed count of infected machines exists.

responses.summary: Confirmed 0.5.144 was published via a compromised maintainer account, disclosed the roughly 100-minute live window, said only npm was affected and no usage was observed, and documented the hostage token behavior with remove-before-revoke workarounds.

Decoded the payload without running it, documented the theft set, self-spread mechanism and dead-man's switch, and published ordered remediation that removes the token monitor before any credential rotation.
Framed the compromise as the Shai-Hulud worm jumping into AI infrastructure.

incidents.name: GhostAction: GitHub campaign adds developer-machine credential stealer

incidents.summary: GitGuardian's Oct 27 follow-up counted 72,026 malicious commits across 22,964 public repositories in the Oct 13-21 wave, adding developer-machine, self-hosted runner and AWS OIDC payloads. It found no successful runs of those malicious workflows; the VS Code stealer is outside that protection. Repository and commit counts are not confirmed theft totals.
incidents.dateLabel: Original wave Sept 2025; resurgence Aug 31-Sep 30, 2026; 30k+ repo burst Oct 8-12, 2026; follow-up covers Oct 13-21 and Oct 22-26 rewrites (reported Oct 27)

sources.label: GitGuardian: October escalation and PolinRider overlap
GitGuardian: GhostAction Returns (772 repos, 30k more in Oct)

incidents.correction: The 2025 and 2026 reports describe waves of the same campaign. Repository targeting figures do not equal successful compromises. See GitGuardian’s report for the effect of GitHub’s workflow blocking. Oct 27 follow-up: the new commit/repository counts are observed lower bounds, not successful executions or stolen-secret counts. GitGuardian found no successful runs of the new malicious workflows. Its developer-machine payload does not use Actions; shared launcher code and co-infected repositories do not establish a shared actor with PolinRider.

detail.whatHappened: GhostAction is a supply chain campaign that injects malicious GitHub Actions workflows into repositories using the victims' own compromised credentials, then harvests the secrets those workflows can reach. GitGuardian first revealed it in September 2025 (817 public repositories across 327 users, at least 3,325 secrets exfiltrated) and now says the campaign never stopped: it tracked activity through late 2025 and into 2026 with shifting exfiltration endpoints. A new wave ran from August 31 to September 30, 2026, pushing the workflow to 772 public repositories belonging to 373 users and organizations and targeting 2,577 secrets; GitHub held most runs for approval, so only 499 of 3,669 collected runs executed, exfiltrating 26 confirmed secrets from 13 repositories. Then between October 8 and 12 the campaign accelerated: more than 30,000 repositories across about 3,000 users and orgs were targeted through roughly 1,900 compromised GitHub accounts, attempting to extract 3,174 secrets. This time the workflows actually ran, and Socket confirmed successful exfiltration on October 8, before GitHub began blocking the malicious workflow from running on October 9, so the October 10 and 12 waves extracted nothing. In its Oct 27 follow-up, GitGuardian counted 72,026 operator commits across 22,964 public repositories, 2,875 owners and 1,792 pushing accounts for the Oct 13-21 wave. Of those accounts, 1,382 had already pushed the Oct 8 payload, consistent with reuse of stolen tokens. These are feed-observed lower bounds. The campaign now has five payload families: re-pointed security-audit workflows, seven new workflow names, self-hosted runner workflows, a Node.js stealer disguised as a font with a VS Code folder-open task, and legacy workflows attempting AWS role access via OIDC. The last GhostAction commit the researchers observed was Oct 21 at 04:37 UTC. Separately, Oct 22-26 rewrites added PolinRider loaders to some GhostAction commits; that is not evidence the GhostAction operator continued pushing after Oct 21.
detail.exposure: Targeted secrets in the 2026 waves include SSH private keys and deployment credentials (446), Azure credentials (218, with one organization exposing an Azure PAT and SSH key across 92 repositories), container registry credentials (142), database credentials (112), AWS access keys (106), FTP credentials (92), Google Cloud and Firebase credentials (80), GitHub tokens (66), and bot tokens plus Cloudflare, npm, PyPI and AI provider keys. The October payload versions also grep the working tree and full git history, with special context capture around AWS key IDs, pointing at intent to hit private repositories too. Confirmed theft counts are much lower than target counts: 26 secrets confirmed exfiltrated in the August-September wave; the October wave's confirmed exfiltration is established by Socket's analysis but without a public total. Victims from earlier waves were hit again, suggesting reliance on unrotated secrets stolen months or years ago. The Oct 27 report describes payloads aimed at local cloud, registry, AI-tool, SSH and Kubernetes credentials on developer machines and self-hosted runners, plus AWS roles reachable through OIDC. The fake-font task runs when the affected folder is opened in VS Code and the workspace is trusted; 17,667 repositories carried that file pair. GitGuardian found no successful runs of the new malicious workflows, and says the self-hosted family originally had a YAML error. The endpoint stealer does not use Actions, so GitHub's workflow blocking does not protect developer machines from it. The report does not establish an endpoint infection count or a new stolen-secret total.
detail.fix: GitHub began preventing the malicious workflow from running starting October 9, which blocked later malicious workflow runs, not every subsequent payload or developer-machine attack. Cleanup is visible but incomplete: only 124 of 772 repositories in the August-September wave (16%) had removed the workflow in public history by October 5, and in 92 cases the attacker simply re-pointed old, never-removed workflows at the new endpoint. Affected users need to remove the injected workflow (names include github_actions_security.yml and security-audit.yml), rotate every secret referenced in their CI, and check for runs of the injected workflows. GitGuardian and StepSecurity published the exfiltration indicators, including the IP 193.32.204.199 and earlier endpoints. For the newer wave, GitGuardian advises removing all injected files on every branch rather than reverting update commits that restore an older malicious version; revoking compromised account access and rotating repository, history, Actions and wiki secrets; checking private gists named build cache containing c.dat; and inspecting affected developer machines and self-hosted runners for persistence. Three payload families attempt a crontab entry marked #ghc2 that fetches code every five minutes; repository cleanup alone does not remove host persistence if a payload ran. Audit AWS CloudTrail for unexpected AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity activity and restrict OIDC trust to intended repositories and branches. Inspect VS Code folderOpen tasks and font files that are actually scripts.
detail.remaining: Attribution is unknown. The full count of secrets stolen in the October wave has no public total. How the roughly 1,900 GitHub accounts were originally compromised is not established, though reuse of previously stolen credentials is the documented pattern. GitGuardian also found a cryptominer injected into kuafuai/DevOpsGPT by the same compromised account days before the new wave, but its analysis concludes the miner is probably a different actor exploiting the same stolen account - an illustration that stolen credentials do not have a single owner. The Oct 27 report does not establish a common operator for GhostAction and PolinRider: copied launchers, overlapping repositories and 188 rewritten GhostAction commits are evidence of overlap, not shared attribution. GitGuardian's working hypothesis is copied public launcher code and overlapping stolen tokens. Its feed cannot establish total scope, and endpoint execution, host persistence and AWS role access are not confirmed simply by finding these payloads in repositories.

responses.summary: Reported 72,026 commits across 22,964 public repositories in the Oct 13-21 wave, five payload families and later PolinRider-loader rewrites. Found no successful new malicious workflow runs, distinguished developer-endpoint exposure from Actions blocking, and published host, token and OIDC cleanup guidance without claiming a shared actor.

Published the campaign history and the 2026 waves: 772 repositories and 2,577 targeted secrets in August-September, the October 8-12 burst targeting 30,000-plus repositories through about 1,900 compromised accounts, payload evolution toward git-history scanning, execution statistics, cleanup rates, and the DevOpsGPT cryptominer caveat.

incidents.name: Eight eMudhra CA keys were crackable from public certificates
incidents.subject: eMudhra
incidents.summary: Eight eMudhra intermediate certificate-authority keys were weak enough to recover from public certificates, including one with the value 4. eMudhra revoked them. Its account says none issued end-entity certificates; this is not a confirmed breach of its infrastructure.
incidents.dateLabel: Reported Oct 17; vendor revised revocation date to Oct 18; public Oct 20-22, 2026

sources.label: Google: Protecting Chrome and Android users
The Register: eMudhra defends its keys
Go Security team: our response to the eMudhra key disclosure incident
eMudhra press release: no impact across Middle East and Africa (Oct 26)
Microsoft MSRC: response to compromised eMudhra CA keys (updated Oct 27)
Cloudflare follow-up: exploitation tracking and patching telemetry

incidents.correction: The vendor describes weak-key revocation rather than an infrastructure breach. Tailscale, Node.js and Go updates are downstream responses, not additional breaches. Detailed timing and scope are in the vendor statement and Cloudflare report. Timeline note: the official statement was revised by Oct 22 from report Oct 18 / revoke Oct 19 to report Oct 17 / revoke Oct 18. The earlier dates were accurately captured from its prior version; this index now attributes the new dates to the revised vendor account.

detail.whatHappened: In April 2025 eMudhra, an Indian certificate authority, ran a key ceremony that produced eight intermediate CA certificates with badly weak private keys. A researcher found they could be recovered from the public certificates (some keys were single or double digit numbers, one reportedly just 4). He reported it to Mozilla, Chrome, Apple and Microsoft on Oct 17, 2026. In its statement as revised on Oct 22, eMudhra dates revocation to Oct 18. An earlier version of the same statement dated revocation to Oct 19. Mozilla independently dates the initial report to Oct 17; the vendor revision, rather than an independently inspected revocation record, is the basis for the revised revocation day.
detail.exposure: Anyone who worked out the keys could have forged a trusted certificate for any website, but only against software that does not check Certificate Transparency or revocation lists. Chrome and Google say no certificates chaining to these intermediates had been logged to CT, so CT-enforcing browsers could not have been attacked. Cloudflare's Oct 30 follow-up telemetry still shows no confirmed interception: a week of logging on its outbound connections recorded about 22,000 attempted handshakes presenting the weak keys, two-thirds fetches of test sites and almost all the rest origins that appear to have made a certificate for themselves with the weak intermediate. About 160 handshakes carried forged certificates naming other organizations' domains, including consumer IoT names, some valid for over two years; Cloudflare assesses these looked like the servers' own default certificates rather than interception attempts, since the same certificate appeared from many of its locations and the names failed hostname verification anyway. One forged certificate was dated Oct 20 18:19 UTC, under an hour after Mozilla's bug report went public, so forging began within hours of disclosure. Cloudflare says this does not exclude carefully targeted interception and that it has seen no indirect signals of compromise. The 'eight keys' were six TLS intermediates and two code-signing intermediates.
detail.fix: Mozilla blocked them via OneCRL on Oct 17 (done for standard Firefox users by 22:59 UTC) and shipped Firefox 158.0.1, ESR 115.43.1 and 153.5.1, plus NSS 3.131.1 removing the signing root. Chrome blocked them by CRLSet the same day, and removed the emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from its root store. Microsoft blocked the affected intermediates through a Windows Disallowed Certificate Trust List update (Oct 20) and a separate Edge and WebView2 CRLSet update, and on Oct 26 released an out-of-band Windows update removing six eMudhra G3 roots and an AAA Certificate Services cross-sign from the Windows trust list, and on Oct 27 removed the same seven from the Microsoft Edge trust list (confirmed in an Oct 27 MSRC update; the changes reach devices as updates propagate). The reporter also says Apple blocked the certificates; its exact update date was not independently verified here. Cloudflare, Node.js and Tailscale shipped updates, and Go shipped 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 (Oct 19) to reject the intermediates. In Update 4 on Oct 22, eMudhra offered Sectigo-issued certificates as an alternate option for all customers and said its G1 roots remain active and supported. CertiNext users can request this through their account; other customers should use the support route in the official statement.
detail.remaining: Software that ships its own trust store or ignores revocation needs updates. eMudhra has not confirmed a root cause; it says a wrap/unwrap step created a second weak key set. It says seven of the eight were never used and the eighth issued no certificates. It says one US customer ecosystem needs replacement certificates. Investigation ongoing; MeitY has set up a probe panel. Go says Linux revocation-support work is planned but not delivered. eMudhra's Oct 26 regional press release says it will publish a root-cause analysis later. Microsoft's trust-list root removals are a broader trust decision than the intermediate revocations; the Edge trust-list removal is confirmed complete as of Oct 27, and Microsoft is evaluating the remaining eMudhra roots separately. Cloudflare says all its high-priority systems are patched, with a small number of confirmed low-impact tickets still being worked. Its visitor-patching numbers come from 50 million probes on a fraction of its challenge pages over the week, a sample Cloudflare stresses is skewed by unconfirmed bots and limited to JavaScript-executing clients, so it is not an internet-wide measure: within that sample, modern browsers are mostly patched, embedded browsers such as Android WebView lag at 30-40% still accepting, and more than half of probes across large networks still accept the compromised chain, with patching progress flat after the first weekend. An apparent late-week patching jump among Chrome 150-154 on macOS was a bot-traffic classification change, not real patching; declining acceptance on Chrome for Linux is the suggestive exception. Cloudflare also reports eMudhra has announced it is exiting the public CA business and has blamed a mistake in a key generation script it has not shared, and that eMudhra first signed a CRL with what may have been a correctly generated key before correcting it to one signed with the weak key; it says the role of auditors and cross-signers still needs clearing up.

responses.summary: Says keys were revoked, no certificates issued from them, no data breached, signing/eSign services unaffected, key ceremony flaw not yet fully explained. Offers backup CA to enterprise TLS customers.
Received report Oct 17 20:06 UTC, blocked within hours, shipped Firefox and NSS updates.
Blocked by CRLSet Oct 17, removed the signing root from Chrome Root Store, says CT-enforcing clients were not exposed.
Patched WARP, cloudflared, CDN and Zero Trust; found no active exploitation on its services; lists customer actions.
Lists the eight intermediates with hashes and notes eMudhra stopped issuing under its G3 root.

Offers Sectigo-issued certificates as an alternate option for all customers. Says G1 roots remain active and supported. Its updated statement also revises the report/revocation chronology; earlier captured dates are retained as a correction note.

Shipped Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 on Oct 19 (its first URGENT-track release), which reject certificates chaining to the eight intermediates. Go says Linux has no built-in revocation mechanism, so it blocked trust in the runtime; Linux revocation support is planned, not delivered. Rebuild binaries with the patched versions.

responses.by: eMudhra, Middle East and Africa press release
responses.summary: Says no customer or service in the Middle East and Africa was affected, and that impact is confined to one US customer ecosystem. Sectigo certificates are offered at no cost as a redundancy option, not a required fix. Says its root-cause review of key generation and operational controls is ongoing and the RCA will be published later. This is a regional statement, not a global all-clear.

Blocked the eight affected intermediates via a Windows Disallowed Certificate Trust List update (Oct 20) and a separate Edge/WebView2 CRLSet update delivered as an automatic component update. On Oct 26 released an out-of-band Windows update removing six eMudhra G3 roots and an AAA Certificate Services cross-sign from the Windows trust list; on Oct 27 it removed the same seven from the Edge trust list (confirmed in an Oct 27 update to the post). Stresses root removal is a separate, broader trust decision than revoking the compromised intermediates, and that remaining eMudhra roots are under separate evaluation. Advises keeping automatic updates flowing and replacing dependent certificates.

Bulletin 2026-150-AWS (updated Oct 30, 13:45 PDT): Lambda managed runtimes used by ZIP packages have all been updated with fixes, applied in two phases - Phase 1 when a function is created or updated (UpdateFunctionCode or UpdateFunctionConfiguration), Phase 2 automatic updates to functions on Auto runtime update mode; AWS recommends moving Manual or Function Update mode functions to Auto, and container-image functions should be rebuilt and redeployed from the latest image. New AWS Managed Windows Server AMIs include Microsoft's updated trusted root certificate payload via out-of-band Microsoft Update Catalog updates (current even for instances that cannot reach Microsoft's update service or have CTL updates disabled), but existing instances are not changed by the new AMIs - launch new instances from the latest AMIs or apply the Microsoft updates directly. CodeBuild is releasing updated curated images and AMIs beginning Oct 30 (affected roots removed from the OS trust store, Java trust store and AWS CLI, with updated Node.js and Go): projects on the latest curated image receive the fix on their next build, pinned image versions must be updated to the latest, custom images built from curated images must be rebuilt, and builds using their own CA bundle (for example certifi) should update it. EKS released updated AL2023 AMIs (v20261023) and Auto Mode AMIs. Application Load Balancer is removing the affected roots from OIDC/JWT trust stores Oct 29-31, with newly created load balancers protected by Nov 2. AWS SDK for Python (boto3/botocore): update to 1.43.117 or later. RDS for SQL Server targeted Oct 30 (no customer action), EMR updated versions targeted Oct 31, Amplify Node 22/24 patches expected in all regions by Oct 31. Bottlerocket AMIs at or below v1.67.0 remain affected until updated AMIs are available; an interim per-node trust override is published. CloudFront edge CA bundle root removal is still stated as deploying toward its Oct 28 target date, not confirmed complete.

A week after the incident: about 22,000 weak-key handshakes logged on its outbound connections, mostly test sites and self-made certificates; about 160 forged certificates naming unrelated domains looked like server defaults, not interception of Cloudflare connections, and no indirect compromise signals were seen, though targeted interception cannot be excluded. Forging began within an hour of the Mozilla bug becoming public. All high-priority Cloudflare systems patched, a few low-impact tickets open. 50 million challenge-page probes (bot-skewed, JavaScript-only sample) show modern browsers mostly patched, Android WebView 30-40% still accepting, and more than half of probes on large networks still accepting.

Hacker News discussion with Railway employee comments

incidents.correction: Railway's preliminary report now gives an upper bound (1.85% of workspaces, ~100,000, some variables potentially compromised), not a confirmed count of impacted customers; the final forensic report is still pending. The deployment pause was precautionary and builds are restored.

detail.whatHappened: On the morning of October 21, 2026, Railway detected anomalous activity in the systems that store customer environment variables. It disclosed that an unauthorized third party may have accessed those encrypted variables and, for some customers, obtained the decrypted contents. Railway says it believes the attack is part of a series targeting platform companies with the aim of compromising AI inference providers, and it asked those providers to revoke keys proactively. A Railway employee wrote on Hacker News that preliminary forensics point to AI credentials as the attacker's primary goal and called the attacker highly motivated, while cautioning that a formal postmortem is still pending and that the company balanced its duty to warn against the risk of messaging before exploit paths were closed. Railway has not said how the attacker got in. Railway's preliminary report, published Oct 22 and linked from the status page on Oct 23, dates the attack window to Oct 20 13:58 UTC-Oct 22 03:32 UTC and says the attacker sought AI provider API keys for distillation attacks. According to that report, the attacker pulled secrets in encrypted form, then used credentials taken from Railway's CI environment to decrypt a subset of them.
detail.exposure: Secrets customers stored as environment variables: API keys, database passwords and private registry credentials. Railway says its initial analysis suggests the impact may be limited to a subset of users, but it has not given a count of affected accounts. Separately, individuals reported on X and Hacker News that AI keys stored on Railway were drained in real time, and the founder of Postiz said he took that service offline after Anthropic and Stripe warned that its keys were compromised. Those are individual reports, not Railway findings. Railway has not said that consumers' personal data was taken. The preliminary report quantifies the ceiling: at most 1.85% of all workspaces (about 100,000) had some environment variables potentially compromised; Railway stresses this is an upper bound, not a count of confirmed customer impact, and says it is notifying definitely impacted and high-risk customers directly. It says the attacker did not access Railway user accounts, and does not rule out access to user source code, to be confirmed in the final forensic report. Railway asked GitHub, GitLab, Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, SpaceXSI and Stripe to revoke potentially compromised keys, and supplied some vendors with all keys on the platform, so a vendor revocation notice does not by itself prove impact.
detail.fix: Railway initially paused deployments and advised all users to rotate environment variables, API keys and private registry credentials and review logs. It reset bucket S3 credentials and its held GitHub account tokens; services need new bucket credentials and a redeploy, and GitHub account connections need reconnecting. Importantly, GitHub registry personal-access tokens removed from Railway may still work on GitHub: users must revoke and replace those at GitHub too. Its official recovery guide distinguishes these actions. As of the status update at Oct 22 22:49 UTC (page still marked Identified), Railway reported builds enabled for Free and Trial as well as Hobby, Pro and Enterprise, with builds and deployments on all five plans at approximately normal speed. New signups remained temporarily paused. The Railway API was restored earlier on Oct 22, and API tokens and Project Tokens created before the incident remain invalidated, so users of the Public API or CLI must create new tokens. Check the status page before relying on that snapshot. In the preliminary report Railway recommends that all users who signed up before Oct 21 revoke and reapply sensitive environment variables, remove public network access to databases, check GitHub account audit logs and app access, and review audit logs in registries such as Docker Hub. Builds are restored on all plans, but the report is preliminary and the final forensic report is still pending. As of the Oct 23 19:18 UTC status update the incident is in Monitoring: notifications to higher-risk workspaces are complete, but Railway explicitly says workspaces outside those groups are not confirmed safe, so the rotation guidance still stands for anyone who has not acted. Rotations completed since containment need not be repeated because of this notice alone.
detail.remaining: The entry point and the final affected-account count are still undisclosed; the preliminary report gives only an upper bound (1.85% of workspaces, about 100,000, potentially compromised) and promises a final forensic report. Whether user source code was accessed is explicitly not ruled out. Platform operations were marked resolved on Oct 23 22:06 UTC, but Railway says workspaces outside the higher-risk notification groups are not confirmed safe, so credential rotation guidance still stands for anyone who has not acted. Downstream access to customers' application databases has not been established. incidents.name: LiteLLM 1.107.0 shipped a credential stealer via PyPI and Docker
incidents.subject: LiteLLM
incidents.summary: LiteLLM confirms its release pipeline pushed malicious 1.107.0 packages to PyPI and container registries. The malware stole credentials and loaded remote-code tools. Affected artifacts were removed; private enterprise releases were not impacted.
incidents.correction: This is the October 1.107.0 compromise, separate from the earlier 2026 1.82.x incident. The official advisory lists affected registry tags and the exposure windows.

detail.whatHappened: In the early morning of October 21, 2026, LiteLLM's release pipeline was compromised and pushed a malicious version 1.107.0 to PyPI and to Docker Hub and GHCR. The package contained compiled malware: a credential stealer that runs every time Python starts, plus a remote-code loader backdoor. LiteLLM's canonical root-cause report (Oct 23, investigation complete) traces the chain: on May 27, 2026 a configuration file containing the master key of a LiteLLM Agent Platform deployment was committed to the public LiteLLM-Labs/lite-harness repository; the error was spotted and force-pushed over, but the master key was never revoked. On October 10 the attacker used that key against the Agent Platform API and retrieved an unscoped GitHub CLI OAuth token belonging to a GitHub organization owner, then pushed throwaway CI branches (ci-tmp-a351cc, ci-tmp-be33e9) whose workflows posted two more maintainers' GitHub CLI tokens (GH_TOKEN and RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN) to an attacker-controlled endpoint. On October 21 the attacker repointed the private project-releaser workflow at a lookalike repository (Berri-AI/litellm instead of BerriAI/litellm) - the push with a maintainer token was rejected by branch protection, so the owner's token was used to override it - triggered the release with one stolen token, approved the production gate with another (the release approval rule had been relaxed that week from a physical-device-locked account to any two engineers), and let the normal signing pipeline publish the poisoned artifacts. The attacker then deleted the workflow run records and force-pushed the releaser's main back to hide the change. This corrects LiteLLM's initial assumption, carried in its Oct 21 post, that the tokens were harvested from logs of an internal LiteLLM deployment exposed to the internet; the canonical report states the first token came from the Agent Platform API instead. This is LiteLLM's second supply chain compromise of 2026; Datadog linked the earlier March incident (versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8) to TeamPCP and says no connection between the two has been established.
detail.exposure: Anyone who ran pip install on litellm 1.107.0 between 11:39 and 13:23 UTC on October 21, or started the v1.107.0, latest, main-latest or main-stable Docker Hub images between 11:46 and 14:20 UTC (affected GHCR tags were unavailable by 13:51 UTC). The stealer collected cloud credentials (AWS, GCP, Azure, including instance metadata), Kubernetes, Docker, Vault and Terraform secrets, SSH, GPG and TLS keys, Git, npm and PyPI tokens, .env files, shell history, LLM provider API keys, AI coding tool sessions, browser saved passwords and cookies, and credentials stored in a LiteLLM proxy database. Data went encrypted to the lookalike domain www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck. The backdoor polled a fixed GitHub-hosted file hourly for a new domain; Datadog says that file only ever held test values, so no second-stage payload was observed in the wild. Enterprise customers on LiteLLM's private registry were not affected, and the official 1.107.0 source tag on GitHub is clean.
detail.fix: Affected artifacts were removed or repointed on Oct 21. LiteLLM recommends an explicit clean pin such as 1.106.2. On an affected host, follow the vendor's ordered cleanup before running Python or pip: startup hooks can re-execute the malware. Remove persistence, rebuild from trusted images, then rotate every credential the host or proxy database could reach. Do not treat uninstalling the package as complete cleanup.
detail.remaining: The number of users who installed the malicious artifacts has not been published. The investigation into the attack chain is complete per LiteLLM's Oct 23 canonical report, which also says the attacker focused on upstream inference API tokens and that LiteLLM is revoking every token across its internal systems and vendor platforms; a process-improvements post is promised for the following week.

responses.summary: Published a detailed incident post with the attack chain, exact compromise windows, artifact digests, cleanup steps and a promise of updates every two hours; status marked contained with investigation in progress.

Independently analyzed the payload: a Python-startup credential stealer exfiltrating to a lookalike domain plus an hourly remote-code loader whose second stage was never observed live; noted this is LiteLLM's second 2026 compromise with no established link to the March TeamPCP incident.

LiteLLM published the canonical root-cause analysis, superseding assumptions in its Oct 21 post: the entry point was an unrevoked Agent Platform master key committed to the public LiteLLM-Labs/lite-harness repo on May 27, used on Oct 10 to pull the org owner's unscoped GitHub CLI OAuth token from the Agent Platform API - not token harvesting from internal deployment logs. Throwaway CI workflows exfiltrated two more maintainer tokens; the attacker repointed the release workflow at lookalike fork Berri-AI/litellm, overrode branch protection with the owner's token, triggered and approved the release with the two maintainer tokens, then deleted run records and force-pushed history to cover tracks. Indicators published: IPs 69.48.229.143 and 199.91.221.39, fork commit 20535d8f, releaser commits 9cf97e9 and 285fbdc5, branches ci-tmp-a351cc and ci-tmp-be33e9.

The claim omits that Docker Hub and GHCR tags were also compromised for a slightly longer window.

incidents.name: OpenCode breach exposes users' AI provider keys
incidents.subject: OpenCode
incidents.summary: OpenCode confirmed a security breach affecting 1.4% of Console users during a large-scale attack. Reporting says stored keys for linked AI providers were exposed and some users saw unauthorised charges. The official post confirms the breach, not an audited total of financial losses.
incidents.dateLabel: Exposure reported from 17 Oct 2026; press 19 Oct
incidents.correction: The official OpenCode statement is linked alongside reporting and maintainer commentary. The company described a distillation attack; user charges and wider attribution are not independently audited. Do not treat every linked comment as a confirmed technical finding.

detail.whatHappened: Overnight around October 17-18, 2026, attackers broke into an older OpenCode system and reached stored API keys that some users of the hosted OpenCode Console had linked to external AI providers. OpenCode announced on October 18 that it had suffered a security breach related to a large-scale distillation attack affecting 1.4% of Console users, and said it emailed everyone affected that morning; users without an email were not impacted. Co-founder Dax Raad said attackers had been hitting the company's systems nonstop for at least 48 hours using AI agents, and that the investigation was hampered when the AI models OpenCode was using began refusing to analyze malicious code because of safety filters. The team said things stabilized after OpenAI gave it access to Daybreak, a program offering models vetted for defensive security work. The open source app and CLI were not affected; only the hosted Console stored such keys. The breach happened the same night OpenCode made GLM-5.3-Flash free for users.
detail.exposure: Stored keys for linked providers including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, for the 1.4% subset of Console users who had external providers linked. The notice to impacted users says the earliest possible key exposure was October 17, 2026, 00:30 UTC, and that no other data appears to have been exposed. Users then reported unauthorized charges on Reddit and X, commonly hundreds of dollars and in some cases over 1,000 or 1,700 dollars overnight; some said Google suspended their projects for abusive activity consistent with hijacked resources. Charge figures are user reports, not an audited total.
detail.fix: OpenCode notified affected users by email on the morning of October 18 and told them to revoke and replace their keys directly with each provider. It said it was working with Google, OpenAI and Anthropic. Anthropic and Google blocked the API keys they believed were exposed. OpenAI said it worked with OpenCode to restore access and refund credits used in the attack, and OpenCode said refunds for unauthorized charges were underway, with its email to impacted users mentioning possible reimbursement.
detail.remaining: OpenCode has not explained how attackers gained access to the older system, how the keys were stored, or the full extent of misuse, and said the incident remains ongoing. The distillation framing is OpenCode's own characterization; skeptics quoted by TechCrunch argue the use of stolen keys for distillation is unproven and that this may be a straightforward breach. No audited total of financial losses exists.

responses.summary: Announced the breach tied to a large-scale distillation attack, scoped it to 1.4% of Console users with linked external providers, and said all impacted users were emailed.

Described 48 hours of nonstop attacks by AI agents, safety filters refusing defensive analysis, stabilization after getting OpenAI Daybreak access, and stressed that the open source app's keys never reach OpenCode.
Reported the key exposure, user-reported charges up to about 1,700 dollars, suspended Google Cloud projects, and the reimbursement mention in OpenCode's email.
Reported the older-system breach, provider responses (Anthropic and Google blocking keys, OpenAI refunds), the Daybreak defensive-access angle, and skepticism that the distillation motive is proven.

claimChecks.claim: OpenCode BREACHED. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google API keys exposed for Console users. Distillation attack. Bills run up in $$$$.
claimChecks.explanation: The breach and provider key exposure for a 1.4% subset of Console users are confirmed by OpenCode, and unauthorized charges are real user reports (hundreds to over a thousand dollars). The distillation attack framing comes from OpenCode itself and remains unproven to outside skeptics; charge totals are user-reported, not audited.

incidents.name: PHP2Shell: two critical 9.2 RCE flaws in PHP core
incidents.subject: PHP
incidents.summary: PHP fixed two critical core bugs, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. The PHP team rates both 9.2 and urges immediate updates. All web-serving PHP installations need review, with the highest demonstrated risk in Apache mod_php.
incidents.dateLabel: Disclosed / fixed 21 Oct 2026

sources.label: JFrog Security Research: PHP2Shell - all you need to know

incidents.correction: This is a vulnerability and patch advisory, not proof that every PHP installation was breached. CISA advises taking systems offline if they cannot be patched or run PHP 8.1 or older; it does not tell every patched site to go offline.

detail.whatHappened: Two memory-handling bugs in PHP itself can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. One involves out-of-memory cleanup; the other leaves stale state for a later request in the same worker. PHP released fixes on Oct 21. The PHP project uses the CVE identifiers; php2shell is the researchers' name.
detail.exposure: PHP rates both CVSS v4.0 9.2 (the leaked post claimed 10.0). On Apache mod_php, an unauthenticated request can trigger the first bug before application code runs. Amazon Threat Intelligence (via Tenable) reports exploitation attempts from Oct 17, before disclosure. CISA's Oct 21 alert said it had not itself observed exploitation at publication.
detail.fix: Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35. CISA says take PHP systems offline if you cannot patch or you run PHP 8.1 or older, and that a WAF may give partial protection.
detail.remaining: PHP is embedded in many products, so inventory is hard. End-of-life branches have no official fix except source backports (per Tenable). The PHP Foundation admitted a fix for the underlying out-of-memory problem had stalled for months.

responses.summary: Urges immediate patching; offline if unpatchable or PHP 8.1 and older.
Explains the bugs, credits finders, admits the fix was delayed by decision-making and resources.

incidents.name: Tailscale ships update distrusting eMudhra certificates
incidents.subject: Tailscale
incidents.summary: Tailscale published an emergency update to distrust the compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates. This is a downstream certificate-trust response, not a separate Tailscale breach. WireGuard mesh traffic does not rely on that public certificate trust.
incidents.dateLabel: Bulletin / release 21 Oct 2026
incidents.correction: This is a follow-on to the eMudhra certificate incident, not an independent Tailscale compromise. See bulletin TS-2026-013 and the current changelog.

detail.whatHappened: Tailscale published bulletin TS-2026-013 on the eMudhra keys. Its client trusts whatever the operating system's certificate store trusts, so a forged eMudhra-signed certificate would have been accepted on devices that still trusted those intermediates.
detail.exposure: Only web PKI connections that rely on the system store. Tailscale says node-to-node WireGuard traffic does not use that store and is not affected. No exploitation reported in the bulletin.
detail.fix: Tailscale v1.104.2 or later (built with Go 1.27.3) explicitly distrusts the compromised certificates. Tailscale's own services were updated.
detail.remaining: Devices on older clients with OS stores that still contain the intermediates.

responses.summary: Bulletin TS-2026-013: update to v1.104.2 or later. Listed by Oct 21-22; a per-bulletin publication date was not visible.

sources.label: Node.js blog: Wednesday, October 21, 2026 Security Releases

detail.whatHappened: On Oct 21, 2026 the Node.js project shipped security releases v22.23.4, v24.22.1 and v26.12.1 fixing ten CVEs and updating bundled c-ares, OpenSSL (24.x, 22.x), SQLite (22.x), Undici and the CA certificate list to drop the eMudhra intermediates.

detail.fix: None reported.
