detail.remaining: The draft report is unpublished, so Cathedral's claims are unverified beyond what Anthropic confirms. Whether Cathedral's activity stayed within bug-bounty scope is contested. The episode undercuts both easy narratives: autonomous agents reached a leading AI lab's business systems in hours, and the loudest version of the claim comes from the people selling the capability.

responses.summary: Confirmed receiving the findings via bug bounty, says reach was limited to sales, HR and IT systems, denies impact to Claude conversations, source code and model weights, cut access same-day, and accuses Cathedral of violating bounty rules by withholding activity.
Claims its AI agents reached meeting transcripts, salary and offer data, and Slack discussions about advanced models within 12 hours by abusing third-party business software weaknesses.

claimChecks.claim: AI agents hacked Anthropic in under 12 hours
claimChecks.explanation: Anthropic confirms an intrusion path into some business systems existed and was closed the same day. The claimed depth (transcripts, salaries, model Slack) is Cathedral's and disputed by Anthropic; core systems (conversations, code, weights) were not affected per Anthropic.

incidents.name: CVE-2026-97631: 16-year-old pre-boot RCE in TianoCore EDK II threatens most servers via PXE boot
incidents.subject: TianoCore EDK II (UEFI firmware)
incidents.summary: A buffer overflow in the PXE boot driver of TianoCore EDK II - the open-source UEFI code underneath most server firmware from AMI, Insyde and Phoenix - lets an attacker on the local network hang the boot or, with knowledge of the firmware build, execute code at the highest privilege before Secure Boot applies. Found by Anthropic and Google researchers, it went public months early after AMI published a fix, breaking the planned January disclosure embargo.
incidents.dateLabel: Fix PR public Oct 14, 2026 (embargo broken; planned disclosure was January); Ars Technica Oct 27, oss-security Oct 28

sources.label: oss-security: CVE-2026-97631 pre-boot RCE in EDK II PXE driver

incidents.correction: Only machines that boot over the network (PXE) are exposed, and code execution needs knowledge of the target's firmware build; an attacker otherwise gets a boot hang. This is not remote-from-the-internet: it needs local network access during boot.

detail.whatHappened: A 16-year-old buffer overflow (CVE-2026-97631) sits in the NetworkPkg UefiPxeBcDxe driver of TianoCore EDK II, the open-source UEFI implementation that most server vendors ship through firmware suppliers such as AMI, Insyde and Phoenix. An attacker with local network access can send an oversized ICMP error message to a machine while it boots over the network (PXE), hanging the boot process or - if the target's firmware build is known - running code at the highest privilege level, before Secure Boot and the OS's defenses exist. The flaw was found by Anthropic and Google researchers. It became public months ahead of a planned January disclosure when AMI published a code fix, forcing organizations to chase firmware updates from their individual vendors.
detail.exposure: Most servers worldwide carry EDK II-derived firmware, but the exploitable surface is narrower: only machines configured for network boot, and only from the local network during the boot window. Data centers using PXE provisioning at scale are the real risk population.
detail.fix: The upstream fix is tianocore/edk2 PR #13302 (public since Oct 14). Because EDK II reaches machines through firmware suppliers, remediation means firmware updates from each server vendor; there is no OS-level patch. Where firmware updates are pending, disabling unused PXE boot removes the exposure.
detail.remaining: Which vendors have shipped patched firmware, and for which models, is untracked centrally. Whether the broken embargo leaves a usable exploit window is unquantified - no in-the-wild exploitation has been reported.

responses.summary: Fix merged upstream as PR #13302; AMI's early publication of its code fix broke the coordinated January embargo and made the flaw public.

claimChecks.claim: The flaw threatens most servers on the planet
claimChecks.explanation: EDK II-derived firmware ships in most servers, but exploitation requires local network access and PXE network boot, and reliable code execution needs the target's firmware build. The at-risk set is PXE-booted machines, not every server.

incidents.name: Cloudflare Workers AI cross-tenant leak: 155 GLM-5.3 responses carried other customers' data
incidents.subject: Cloudflare
incidents.summary: A configuration mismatch (KV cache smaller than the advertised context window) plus an SGLang bug let over-length requests to GLM-5.3 on Workers AI read cache data left by other customers' sessions. Cloudflare says 155 responses between Aug 27 and Sep 9 were affected, all with prompts over 681,280 tokens; it found no evidence of deliberate exploitation, fixed the issue after a HackerOne report, and SGLang shipped the fix in 0.5.22.
incidents.dateLabel: Leak window Aug 27 - Sep 9, 2026; reported via HackerOne (Knostic's Gadi Evron); Cloudflare disclosure and fix Oct 26; SGLang fix in 0.5.22
incidents.correction: 155 affected responses over a two-week window, all tied to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens on one model - not a general Workers AI leak. Cloudflare reports no evidence of deliberate exploitation.

detail.whatHappened: Between August 27 and September 9, 2026, 155 responses from the GLM-5.3 model on Cloudflare's Workers AI platform contained data from other customers' recent requests to the same model. The cause was a configuration mismatch that left the model's KV cache smaller than its advertised context window, combined with a bug in the SGLang inference engine that allowed over-length requests (longer than 681,280 tokens) to read cache data left behind by earlier sessions. Knostic researcher Gadi Evron reported the issue through HackerOne; Cloudflare fixed it and disclosed on October 26.
detail.exposure: Fragments of other tenants' prompts and context returned inside model responses - a cross-tenant data leak inside a hosted AI inference service. Cloudflare counts 155 affected responses, all on GLM-5.3 and all involving very long prompts, and says it found no evidence anyone exploited the condition deliberately.
detail.fix: Cloudflare corrected the configuration and patched its deployment; the upstream SGLang fix shipped in version 0.5.22, and Cloudflare recommends SGLang operators update. The disclosure credits the HackerOne report and coordinates with SGLang.
detail.remaining: What data actually appeared in the 155 responses is not enumerated, and affected customers' notification status is not described in the public posts. Other hosted SGLang deployments may have the same bug until they update.

responses.summary: Published a full root-cause and remediation post: configuration mismatch plus SGLang bug, 155 affected responses, no evidence of deliberate exploitation, fix deployed, coordinated with SGLang on the 0.5.22 upstream fix.
Reported the cross-tenant exposure via HackerOne and published a research write-up on the KV-cache reuse condition.

incidents.name: University of Copenhagen breach: data of ~525,000 people, incl. national ID numbers and 20k card PINs
incidents.subject: University of Copenhagen
incidents.summary: Hackers reached one of the university's test environments and took personal data on about 525,000 current and former members - names, phone numbers, personal emails, and CPR national identity numbers for many - plus the PIN codes for roughly 20,000 staff and student ID cards, since reissued. Detected and contained Oct 20; attacker and motive unknown.
incidents.dateLabel: Attack detected and contained Oct 20, 2026; disclosed Oct 23; card PINs reissued after disclosure

sources.label: University of Copenhagen news · Original source

incidents.correction: The 525,000 figure covers current and former members of the university community whose data sat in the compromised test environment; CPR numbers were included for many, not all, and the 20,000 PINs are for university ID cards, not payment cards.

detail.whatHappened: The University of Copenhagen says attackers gained access to one of its test environments and obtained personal data on about 525,000 current and former members of the university community. The attack was detected on October 20, 2026 and contained. The university disclosed the breach on October 23.
detail.exposure: Names, phone numbers and personal email addresses, along with Danish national identity (CPR) numbers for many of those affected - CPR numbers are the sensitive core, since they enable identity fraud. The PIN codes for the ID cards of roughly 20,000 staff and students were also compromised and have been reissued.
detail.fix: The university contained the incident on detection, reissued the compromised card PINs, and published a breach notification page with guidance for affected people.
detail.remaining: The university says it does not know who is behind the attack or the motive. Why a test environment held live personal data at this scale, and whether the data has been used or published, is unaddressed publicly.

responses.summary: Disclosed the breach with counts and data categories, confirmed containment, reissued ~20,000 ID-card PINs, and published a notification page for affected people.

incidents.name: FEC takes campaign-finance filing system offline after attempted breach, a week before US midterms
incidents.subject: US Federal Election Commission
incidents.summary: The FEC shut down parts of its electronic filing system after cybersecurity staff noticed attempted intrusions, a person familiar with the situation told POLITICO - in the final week before the November 3 midterms, blocking the 24/48-hour campaign-finance reports. Past filings stayed searchable and the FEC initially declined to explain the outage. The system was restored Oct 28. An attempted intrusion and an availability hit; no data theft is confirmed.
incidents.dateLabel: Attempted breach and shutdown reported Oct 27, 2026; system restored Oct 28; midterms Nov 3
incidents.correction: Reported as attempted intrusions, not a confirmed compromise: the FEC shut the attacked components down to contain them, and no data theft or alteration has been established in the sources cited.

detail.whatHappened: The Federal Election Commission's electronic filing system went offline in the final week before the November 3, 2026 midterm elections. POLITICO reports, from a person familiar with the situation granted anonymity to discuss an ongoing internal investigation, that FEC cybersecurity staff 'noticed attempted intrusions and were able to shut down' the parts of the filing system being attacked, describing the incident as 'quite narrow and compartmentalized.' The Washington Post had earlier reported the system down with the agency declining to say why. The outage blocked the 24-hour and 48-hour reports that track last-minute campaign spending on specific races, while past filings remained searchable. Some systems remained down through Tuesday evening, October 27; the system was restored on October 28.
detail.exposure: Availability, not (so far) data: campaigns and political groups could not file required last-minute spending disclosures during the outage. No theft or modification of filings has been reported. The FEC does not administer elections or count ballots, so voting itself is unaffected.
detail.fix: FEC cybersecurity staff shut down the attacked parts of the filing system to contain the attempt, and service was restored on October 28. The agency initially declined public comment on the cause.
detail.remaining: Who attempted the intrusion, what they reached before the shutdown, and why the agency would not initially explain the outage are unanswered in the reporting. Whether any filing deadlines were formally extended is unconfirmed.

responses.summary: Cybersecurity staff noticed the attempted intrusions early, shut down the attacked components ('quite narrow and compartmentalized'), and restored the system October 28; the agency had declined to explain the outage when first asked.

incidents.name: Northflank breach: customer environment variables decrypted, stored AI API keys abused
incidents.subject: Northflank
incidents.summary: Northflank, a cloud deployment platform, told all customers on Oct 30 to assume their environment variables have been decrypted and to rotate every secret immediately. Users report unauthorised use of AI API keys stored on the platform, and Northflank links the activity to the 'Black October' wave of attacks on AI developer platforms tracked by Wiz. In a Nov 6 update Northflank said the first known decryption of secrets happened between 02:39 and 03:08 UTC on Oct 30 - more than eight hours before its first security platform alert at 11:43 UTC - that the exploit was patched within 60 minutes of notification and customers were notified within two hours, and that the platform and customer workloads stayed online throughout, with no evidence found so far that workloads or workload data were accessed. Its investigation and an independent forensic review are ongoing, and its rotate-everything guidance still stands.
incidents.dateLabel: Wiz threat alert and first Northflank patches Oct 30, 2026 ~11:43-13:05 UTC; addon secret rotation opened to all customers Oct 31 (MySQL/Redis 13:34, MinIO 22:32, RabbitMQ 23:31 UTC); Nov 2 monitoring update: attack vector believed contained within an hour, no sign workload data accessed; Nov 6 update: first known secret decryption Oct 30 02:39-03:08 UTC, exploit patched within 60 minutes of notification, customers notified within two hours, no evidence workload data accessed, forensic review ongoing

sources.label: Wiz · 'Black October' for AI Developer Platforms

detail.whatHappened: On October 30, 2026 at 11:43 UTC Northflank received a threat alert from Wiz and began patching its network policies within the hour, with Wiz's incident response team engaged by 13:00 UTC. At 13:58 UTC Northflank told all users to assume every environment variable stored on the platform had been decrypted and to rotate all keys immediately. By evening it reported that multiple users were confirming unauthorised use of AI API keys they had supplied to the platform, and on October 30 at 23:38 UTC it said the reports 'may be consistent with the broader pattern of attacks targeting AI credentials', pointing at the attacker IP addresses in Wiz's 'Black October' report. The platform saw intermittent degradation over the following days while Northflank rotated its own keys and hardened the platform, and the incident page now sits in monitoring status. In a November 2 update Northflank said it believes the attack vector was contained within an hour of the first alert, that its investigation shows no sign the attacker remained in its environment, and that independent forensic auditors began reviewing the attack over the weekend and continue to review it. It said running workloads were unaffected and it has seen no sign workloads or workload data were accessed - evidence suggests the attack focused on secrets held in its control plane - and that customers on forward-deployed or dedicated control planes are unaffected. It also said it has patched CVE-2026-98432 across its fleet, including BYOC clusters with an active integration, presented as a separate item rather than the identified entry point. Northflank has not yet explained the initial access path; it intends to share a root cause analysis once findings are confirmed. In a November 6 update Northflank published its first timeline of the attack itself: the first known decryption of secrets occurred between 02:39 and 03:08 UTC on October 30, its first security platform alert arrived at 11:43 UTC with engineers responding within minutes, the exploit was patched within 60 minutes of notification, and customers were notified within two hours. It said the platform remained operational and customer workloads stayed online throughout, that the intermittent degradation came during a high volume of simultaneous customer redeployments and during its subsequent key rotation and platform hardening work, and that it has worked with upstream providers to revoke credentials where possible. The investigation and independent forensic review remain ongoing, with further confirmed findings and a root cause analysis promised.
detail.exposure: Potentially every secret stored on Northflank: workload environment variables, secret groups and global secrets - for all customers, including free-tier users. The confirmed harm so far is unauthorised use of stored AI provider keys; Northflank asks users to review their AI provider usage and billing logs. Wiz reports that across this month's campaign, stolen keys are validated within minutes and then used for LLMjacking at scale, and that around $371,000 in cryptocurrency was allegedly taken using keys stored at another breached platform. Northflank's Nov 6 update says it has found no evidence that customer workloads or workload data were accessed and that the platform stayed operational throughout; evidence still suggests the attack focused on secrets held in its control plane - the vendor's own assessment, with the independent forensic review still under way.
detail.fix: Northflank's guidance: revoke and replace every secret stored on the platform with the issuing provider, update the affected secrets and workloads in Northflank, and disable public access on addons where enabled. It has force-enabled secret rotation on Postgres and MongoDB addons, opened secret rotation to all customers for MySQL and Redis (Oct 31 13:34 UTC), MinIO addons (22:32 UTC) and RabbitMQ add-ons (23:31 UTC), enabled audit logs for all customers including free users, and asks anyone seeing suspicious AI key usage to report it to Northflank support and the provider. On Nov 2 it widened the guidance: rotate all secrets now, both integration secrets and project secrets, even without suspicious activity - starting with AI provider keys, cloud provider credentials, payment provider keys, private keys and database credentials - review provider logs for unusual activity, and contact AI providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic directly about unexpected usage or spend. Where it could act on customers' behalf it has revoked Northflank access tokens and sessions, VCS integrations, and cross-account IAM roles and service accounts, so customers should sign in again and reconnect their integrations; customers whose BYOC cluster is no longer connected to Northflank should contact support about the CVE-2026-98432 patch. The Nov 6 update adds two recommendations: users should enable IP restrictions and budget limits wherever available, and Northflank publicly urges upstream providers to offer API endpoints for credential revocation, IP restrictions and enforceable budget limits, saying these controls enable faster incident response and limit the impact of compromised credentials.
detail.remaining: The entry point and full scope are unconfirmed; the Nov 6 timeline establishes when secrets were first decrypted (Oct 30, 02:39-03:08 UTC) but not how the attacker got in, and Northflank says independent forensic auditors are still reviewing and that it will share a root cause analysis once findings are confirmed. Its statements - that the exploit was patched within 60 minutes of notification, that no attacker presence remained, and that no workloads or workload data were accessed - are the vendor's own assessment pending that review, and the incident is in monitoring status, not resolved. Whether the attackers are the same 'agent swarm' behind this month's other AI platform breaches is not established. How many customers' keys were actually abused, and what else the decrypted secrets opened up (databases, addons, downstream SaaS), is unknown. A post-incident report has not been published.

responses.summary: Published the first timeline of the attack: first known decryption of secrets between 02:39 and 03:08 UTC on Oct 30, first security platform alert at 11:43 UTC with engineers responding within minutes, the exploit patched within 60 minutes of notification and customers notified within two hours. Says the platform remained operational and customer workloads stayed online throughout, with no evidence found that workloads or workload data were accessed, and attributes the intermittent degradation to a high volume of simultaneous customer redeployments and its own key rotation and hardening work. Worked with upstream providers to revoke credentials where possible, tells users to rotate all integration and project secrets, review provider logs, and enable IP restrictions and budget limits, and urges upstream providers to offer credential-revocation API endpoints, IP restrictions and enforceable budget limits. Investigation and independent forensic review remain ongoing, with a root cause analysis to follow.

Moved the incident to monitoring: believes the attack vector was contained within an hour of the first alert, reports no sign the attacker remained in its environment, says running workloads were unaffected with no sign workloads or workload data were accessed, and points to secrets in its control plane as the attack's focus. Independent forensic auditors are reviewing, with a root cause analysis promised. Patched CVE-2026-98432 fleet-wide including connected BYOC clusters, revoked access tokens, sessions, VCS integrations and cross-account IAM roles and service accounts where it could act on customers' behalf, and tells all customers to rotate every secret (integration and project) and review provider logs.

Acknowledged the incident the same day, ordered blanket secret rotation, force-enabled Postgres/MongoDB rotation, opened rotation to all customers for MySQL/Redis (Oct 31 13:34 UTC), MinIO (22:32 UTC) and RabbitMQ (23:31 UTC) addons, and enabled audit logs for all customers, and is publishing rolling updates while parts of the platform remain in major outage.

Its threat alert triggered Northflank's response. Its 'Black October' report counts Northflank as the ninth AI developer platform breached this month and describes the shared pattern: targeted theft of stored environment variables feeding LLMjacking and key resale.

claimChecks.claim: Northflank customer environment variables were decrypted
claimChecks.explanation: This is Northflank's own guidance: 'Assume all environment variables have been decrypted. Disable/rotate all keys.' Users have confirmed unauthorised use of stored AI keys.

claimChecks.claim: The Northflank breach is part of the coordinated October campaign against AI platforms
claimChecks.explanation: Wiz lists Northflank as the ninth incident in its 'Black October' campaign tracking and Northflank says attacker IPs overlap, but also notes the incidents are still being analysed and no single root cause links them.

claimChecks.claim: Northflank customer workloads or workload data were accessed in the attack
claimChecks.explanation: Northflank's Nov 6 update says the platform remained operational and customer workloads stayed online throughout, and that it has found no evidence customer workloads or workload data were accessed; customers on forward-deployed or dedicated control planes were unaffected. That remains the vendor's own assessment while independent forensic auditors continue their review; the blanket rotation guidance for control-plane secrets still stands.

claimChecks.claim: The Northflank attack was contained within an hour and the incident is over
claimChecks.explanation: Northflank's Nov 6 update states the exploit was patched within 60 minutes of notification, but also that the first known decryption of secrets happened at 02:39-03:08 UTC on Oct 30 - more than eight hours before its first security platform alert at 11:43 UTC. The patched-within-60-minutes timeline is the vendor's own account, not yet the independent forensic auditors' finding, and the incident page remains in monitoring status with a root cause analysis still pending.

incidents.name: Bunny CDN pulls Armenia node after infrastructure provider intrusion, reissues TLS certificates
incidents.subject: bunny.net
incidents.summary: One of bunny.net's infrastructure providers reported unauthorised access through third-party server management software, and a Bunny CDN node in Armenia sat on an affected server. Bunny cut it from rotation within 20 minutes, wiped it and says neither investigation found evidence the server was actually accessed - but it reissued all platform TLS certificates and is rotating managed customer certificates as a precaution.
incidents.dateLabel: Provider intrusion reported to bunny.net 'last week'; public notice Oct 29, 2026; managed certificate reissuance completed Oct 31 12:50 UTC

detail.whatHappened: An infrastructure provider used by bunny.net reported unauthorised access involving third-party server management software. One Bunny CDN node, located in Armenia, was hosted on a server supplied by that provider. After the alert, bunny.net says its engineers stopped routing traffic through the server within 20 minutes, preserved logs, securely wiped the machine, revoked its access to other systems and permanently removed it from the CDN. Both bunny.net's investigation and the provider's found no evidence the server or its data was accessed, but bunny.net says it cannot completely rule that out. It disclosed the incident publicly on October 29, 2026. The provider is not named.
detail.exposure: If the server was accessed, the potentially exposed data would have been temporarily cached CDN content, Pull Zone configurations and TLS certificates stored on that one node. bunny.net says no account data was stored on the server and no internal systems were affected.
detail.fix: bunny.net revoked and reissued all TLS certificates for its platform domains (b-cdn.net and bunny.run) and completed reissuing all managed custom-domain certificates on Oct 31 12:50 UTC, each with a new private key and the previous certificates revoked; no action is needed from managed-certificate customers. Customers who manage their own TLS certificates are still advised to revoke and reissue them with new private keys as a precaution. bunny.net has stopped using the affected provider while its investigation continues and is changing how configurations are distributed so each PoP only receives the configuration and TLS certificates for the sites it actively serves.
detail.remaining: Whether the attacker ever reached the bunny.net server is unresolved - neither side found evidence of access, but bunny.net explicitly cannot rule it out. The infrastructure provider and the third-party management software are unnamed, and the provider's investigation is still running. It is not stated whether other bunny.net suppliers use the same software.

responses.summary: Contained the affected node within 20 minutes of the provider's alert, disclosed publicly with a plain-English account of what could and could not have been exposed, and rotated all affected certificate material at its own cost rather than waiting for proof of access - managed custom-domain reissuance completed Oct 31 12:50 UTC. It has dropped the affected provider pending its investigation and is reducing what each PoP holds.

claimChecks.claim: Bunny CDN customer data was stolen
claimChecks.explanation: Neither bunny.net's nor the provider's investigation found evidence of access to the server. The certificate rotation is precautionary, and no account data was on the node.

claimChecks.claim: The incident was limited to one CDN node in Armenia
claimChecks.explanation: bunny.net says a single node hosted on the affected provider's server was involved, and that it was permanently removed from the infrastructure.

incidents.name: Akamai warns Linode customers over critical Linux kernel RCE CVE-2026-98432
incidents.subject: Linode (Akamai)
incidents.summary: Akamai opened a customer security advisory for Linode over CVE-2026-98432, a critical (CVSS 9.8) remote, unauthenticated use-after-free in the Linux kernel's IPv4 stack published Oct 15. On Nov 2 Akamai said it has deployed network rules that drop IPv4 packets with optional headers on public and VPC interfaces, which it says eliminates the immediate attack vector, while kernel patch deployment is still continuing. It reported no evidence of exploitation on the Akamai Compute platform as of its Oct 31 update. This is an advisory, not a confirmed breach, and the advisory is not closed.
incidents.dateLabel: CVE-2026-98432 published Oct 15, 2026; Red Hat critical advisory; Akamai/Linode customer advisory opened Oct 30, mitigation work ongoing Oct 31; Nov 2 (10:55 UTC) update: network rules deployed, kernel patches still deploying; AWS bulletin 2026-160-AWS published Oct 30, updated Oct 31: patched Amazon Linux kernels available
incidents.correction: Reached the Hacker News front page as 'Linode Security Incident', but Akamai's advisory describes investigation and mitigation of a published kernel CVE - it explicitly reports no evidence of exploitation on the Akamai Compute platform. An advisory over a critical shared-infrastructure vulnerability, not a confirmed breach.

detail.whatHappened: CVE-2026-98432 is a use-after-free in the Linux kernel's IPv4 networking: tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() transfers ownership of ireq->ireq_opt to the child socket without copying it, and a concurrent CPU processing a retransmitted SYN can then free the same memory. It is remotely exploitable by an unauthenticated attacker and rated CVSS 9.8 (critical); Red Hat issued a critical security bulletin and is expediting fixes. On October 30, 2026 Akamai opened a customer advisory for its Linode cloud platform, saying it was investigating impact, deploying mitigations for the known attack vector, and monitoring the platform in parallel. On November 2, 2026 (10:55 UTC) Akamai updated the advisory: while it continues to deploy kernel patches across its infrastructure, it has also deployed network rules that drop IPv4 packets with optional headers on public and VPC interfaces. Akamai says this eliminates the immediate attack vector, protects its infrastructure and customer workloads without impacting performance or functionality, and is not limited to the MPTCP exploit but targets the underlying vulnerability.
detail.exposure: Any unpatched Linux host accepting IPv4 connections is potentially exposed to remote code execution; for Linode customers that means their own VMs until OS updates are applied. Akamai reports no evidence the vulnerability has been exploited on the Akamai Compute platform.
detail.fix: Apply OS kernel updates from the upstream distribution as soon as they become available - patched Amazon Linux 2 and Amazon Linux 2023 kernels are now available per AWS bulletin 2026-160-AWS (update the kernel and reboot; AWS calls a kernel update plus reboot the only complete remediation). Akamai says it is deploying platform-level mitigations for the known attack vector while it analyses further impact, and points customers at its support tickets for questions. Akamai says the Nov 2 network rules (dropping IPv4 packets with optional headers on public and VPC interfaces) are deployed; kernel patches are still rolling out. It is tracking upstream OS provider security releases and will make updated distributions available as they ship; customers on the Linode-provided kernel should deploy the latest version when it becomes available. Customers should still apply OS updates from their own distribution.
detail.remaining: Akamai's advisory is still open and kernel patch deployment is continuing; the Nov 2 network rules are Akamai's own description of its mitigation, not independently verified, and the advisory is not marked resolved. Akamai's last stated exploitation position (Oct 31) is no evidence of exploitation on the Akamai Compute platform; it has not published a final impact assessment. Vendor kernel fixes are shipping - Amazon Linux 2/2023 per AWS, with Red Hat expediting fixes - but patching plus a reboot remains the customer's responsibility on self-managed hosts.

responses.summary: Said it deployed network rules dropping IPv4 packets with optional headers on public and VPC interfaces, which it says eliminates the immediate attack vector without affecting performance, while kernel patches are still being deployed. Will follow upstream OS releases and advises Linode-kernel users to update when the latest version is available. Provider-specific; separate from other vendors' remediation of the same CVE.

Opened a customer security advisory the day the issue reached it, committed to deploying mitigations for the known attack vector, and is posting progress updates while telling customers to patch their workloads.
Issued critical bulletin RHSB-2026-016 and is expediting kernel fixes across affected releases.

Published security bulletin 2026-160-AWS for the same CVE (Oct 30, updated Oct 31): patched Amazon Linux 2 and Amazon Linux 2023 kernels are available, updated EKS-optimized AL2023 AMIs (v20261031) and ECS-optimized AMIs are rolling out, AWS is updating the infrastructure behind its managed load-balancer/edge services, and it says Lambda is not affected. This is AWS's own platform response to CVE-2026-98432, separate from Akamai's Linode advisory.

claimChecks.claim: Linode was breached
claimChecks.explanation: Akamai's advisory covers investigation and mitigation of a published kernel CVE and says it has no evidence of exploitation on the Akamai Compute platform.

claimChecks.claim: CVE-2026-98432 is remotely exploitable without authentication
claimChecks.explanation: NVD scores it CVSS 9.8 with network attack vector and no privileges required; Red Hat describes a remote, unauthenticated attacker being able to trigger the use-after-free.

incidents.name: Scribd confirms unauthorized access to systems; user emails and partial card metadata exposed
incidents.subject: Scribd (Everand, Slideshare, Fable)
incidents.summary: Scribd, Inc. is notifying users in phases that an unauthorized third party gained access to its systems and reached user information across Scribd, Slideshare, Everand and Fable. incidents.dateLabel: Scribd help-center incident page stamped Oct 1, 2026; user notifications phased via Epiq, at least one received Oct 26, 2026; first wide public discussion Oct 31. Intrusion and discovery dates not stated

sources.label: Scribd Help Center · Information about the recent security incident

incidents.correction: Reached the Hacker News front page on Oct 31 as a fresh 'Tell HN: Scribd Breached', but Scribd's help-center page for the incident predates the thread (stamped October 1, 2026) and notices are being sent in phases - disclosure began earlier in October, and the actual incident date is unstated.

detail.whatHappened: An unauthorized third party gained access to one of Scribd, Inc.'s systems and used that access to reach other internal systems holding user information across Scribd, Slideshare, Everand and Fable. Scribd says it detected the activity, shut down the access, closed the vulnerability, engaged outside forensic and cybersecurity experts, and notified law enforcement and the relevant data protection authorities. detail.exposure: For most accounts, Scribd describes the data as basic account information. The notification email posted to Hacker News specifies: email address, last 4 digits of credit card and country, credit card issuer, card expiry date, and payment history (not including full credit card details). Scribd's help-center page adds that a smaller number of accounts had more sensitive information involved, without saying what. The help-center page's October 1 update stamp versus the phased notifications (at least one received October 26) leaves the disclosure timeline unclear.

incidents.correction: WorkOS says it correlated the researcher's technical evidence against its logs and an independent forensics firm validated the attribution. The researcher said the retrieved data was deleted and not shared; that is an attributed assurance, not an independently published audit of every copy. WorkOS says the affected tool aggregated sales and customer-support system data, and specifies business contact details, account/relationship histories, excerpts from sales calls, support discussions and customer Slack conversations (a limited number of support communications included end-user email addresses), plus product-use and connection/directory-health metadata. It did not disclose affected customer or record counts. Root cause included public internet exposure of the legacy tool API, a weak predictable development credential accepted in production, no API rate limiting, and detection that lagged until after bulk retrieval. WorkOS says it removed public access on Oct 30, removed the weak credential path and revoked/rotated connected-service credentials Oct 30-31, blocked internet access to all internally developed tools Oct 31, verified centralized network logging Nov 2, and began regular ARTEX testing Nov 3. incidents.name: MUJI: up to 27.26M app/store records and 1.09M MUJI Card numbers may have leaked
incidents.subject: MUJI (Ryohin Keikaku)
incidents.summary: Ryohin Keikaku confirmed unauthorized access to its systems around 1:00 AM JST on Oct 29, 2026 and says customer information may have leaked. Its Oct 30 first notice covered up to about 27.26 million MUJI app records (email address, date of birth, gender); the Nov 4 second notice expands that to MUJI online-store members (including non-app users) and adds member IDs to the base set, says about 520,000 of the 27.26 million also include names, addresses and phone numbers, and discloses two card-data groups: about 1.09 million MUJI Card members (full card number, birth date, MUJI Card ID; about 345,000 cards still valid) and about 120 customers who registered cards on the app or store (first 6 + last 2 digits and cardholder name). On Nov 6 Ryohin Keikaku suspended the MUJI online store and almost all app features as a security measure (its third notice on the same incident), estimating 1-2 days; the store was still showing its suspension page as of Nov 9. No dark-web posting or misuse has been confirmed so far.
incidents.dateLabel: Unauthorized access around 1:00 AM JST Oct 29, 2026 (per Credit Saison); first notice Oct 30; second notice Nov 4 expands scope to online-store members and card data; third notice Nov 6 suspends the online store; store still suspended as of Nov 9

detail.whatHappened: Ryohin Keikaku, operator of the MUJI brand, detected unauthorized access to its systems. Card issuer Credit Saison dates the intrusion to around 1:00 AM JST on October 29, 2026. Ryohin Keikaku published a first notice on October 30 saying some customer information held for the official MUJI app may have leaked externally. It says it blocked the access point and applied fixes. On November 4 a second notice reported that further analysis showed the scope includes MUJI online-store members (including people who do not use the app), that some records also contain names, addresses and phone numbers, and that card information for MUJI Card holders and for customers who registered cards on the app or store may also have been accessed. It also confirmed that card numbers, MUJI Card IDs and birth dates collected from Credit Saison before July 2021 for a MUJI points scheme were still held on its systems. On November 6 it suspended the MUJI online store entirely and all MUJI app features except the membership barcode display, citing customer-data protection and further security hardening, estimating a 1-2 day outage; its suspension page was still live on November 9.
detail.exposure: Per Ryohin Keikaku's second-notice table: (1) up to about 27.26 million records (including withdrawn members) of email address, birth date, gender and member ID for MUJI app and online-store customers; (2) about 520,000 of those also include name, address and phone number (as of the notice); (3) about 1.09 million current and former MUJI Card members who joined by July 2021: full card number, MUJI Card ID and birth date, of which about 345,000 cards are currently valid and the rest expired or cancelled - cardholder name, expiry date and security code not included; Credit Saison adds that of the valid cards about 168,000 were viewable together with the base customer info and about 25,000 with the name/address/phone set; (4) about 120 customers who registered card information on the app or online store: first 6 and last 2 digits of the card number plus cardholder name (expiry and security code not included), viewable together with their name/address/phone records. Customers who got a MUJI Card in August 2021 or later are out of scope. Whether any of this data was actually exfiltrated remains unconfirmed: both companies say no dark-web posting and no misuse has been found, and Credit Saison has seen no rise in fraudulent card use.
detail.fix: Ryohin Keikaku says it detected the access, blocked the relevant access point and applied a fix, and is monitoring beyond the affected system. On November 6 it took the online store and almost all app functions offline for further security hardening. It is notifying affected customers individually by email or post. Credit Saison says its own systems were not breached, has stepped up fraud monitoring, offers card reissue on request, and will contact MUJI Card holders whose details Ryohin Keikaku cannot reach. Customers are told to check card statements and watch for impersonation emails and calls.
detail.remaining: Whether data was actually taken (all notices say 'possibility' of leak), the intrusion vector and the full scope are still under investigation; the 520,000 name/address/phone count is marked 'as of now' and may grow. The online store's suspension has run past its 1-2 day estimate (still down November 9) with no new notice yet; the suspension is a stated security measure, not evidence of new exfiltration. Why pre-2021 MUJI Card numbers were still retained on Ryohin Keikaku's systems after the points scheme changed is acknowledged but not explained beyond the notice text.

responses.summary: Disclosed possible leak of email, birth date and gender for up to about 27.26 million MUJI app records, said the access was blocked and fixed, and warned of impersonation emails.

Expanded the scope to online-store members and member IDs, added name/address/phone for about 520,000, and disclosed potential access to MUJI Card numbers (about 1.09 million) and registered-card partial digits (about 120), with a per-category table.

Confirmed about 1.09 million MUJI Card holders in scope (about 345,000 currently valid), said cardholder names, expiry dates and security codes were not included, reported no rise in fraudulent use, and offered reissue.
Suspended the MUJI online store and all app features except the membership barcode as a security measure, estimating 1-2 days to restore; physical stores unaffected.
Reported that about 1.09 million customer records including credit card numbers may have leaked, about 345,000 of them full numbers of currently valid cards with dates of birth.
